title: The AI labor apocalypse is on hold (for now)
key_facts: EL PAÍS argues that fears of an AI job apocalypse are not yet backed by data: employment across the OECD is at historic highs.
It cites official U.S. statistics: AI created about one million jobs in the past year and destroyed about 200,000.
It cites a Stanford University study of job postings in 41 countries: companies using AI most increased employment by 3.3%.
Nobel laureate Simon Johnson (MIT) says the impact so far is more about reorganizing tasks than layoffs; Daron Acemoglu fears worsening inequality.
Experts say to watch entry-level hiring of young graduates rather than overall unemployment rates.

It notes the IMF estimates AI will affect 60% of Western jobs and that Anthropic claims Western unemployment could reach 10% to 20% by 2030; sociologist Manuel Castells calls it suspicious that AI firms sow such fears in their IPO filings.
Experts agree on the need for safety nets; policy ideas include taxing capital less than labor, levies on data centers and universal basic income.
Seven out of 10 Americans believe AI will make finding a job harder, per the article.
quote_evidence: AI created one million jobs in the past year and destroyed about 200,000, according to official U.S. statistics.
A Stanford University study analyzing hundreds of thousands of job postings in 41 countries finds that companies that use AI most have increased employment by 3.3%.

Simon Johnson, Nobel laureate in Economics, tells EL PAÍS from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) that the effects will eventually be felt, but admits that for now the impact is more qualitative (task reorganization) than quantitative (layoffs).
why_it_matters_hint: A long analysis argues the feared AI job losses have not yet shown up in official data, while warning about young graduates and inequality.
notes: Full text read. This is an analysis feature with interviews, not a new study; the statistics are EL PAÍS’s citations and were not checked against the originals.
